sections: Why aggregate results can be misleading

Subgroup evaluation measures model performance separately for meaningful slices of a target population or environment instead of relying only on aggregate accuracy. Hidden stratification can leave rare, clinically or operationally important categories with poor outcomes even when average scores look strong. A subgroup comparison is a diagnostic about sampled conditions, not automatically evidence of discrimination, an unaligned objective or a real-world incident.
Define groups and the population before the audit

Specify the use case, prediction unit, desired target population, labels, decision thresholds and authorized group metadata in a written protocol. Select slices that reflect known risks, deployment sites, time periods, language varieties, acquisition devices or legally and ethically appropriate demographic attributes. Document unknown or missing group labels, overlap and data provenance. Do not infer sensitive attributes from unrelated user data just to construct a dashboard.
Work a synthetic example that exposes the gap

Imagine 100 completely synthetic test cases: group A contains 90 and is correct on 81, so accuracy is 90%; group B contains 10 and is correct on four, so accuracy is 40%. Pooled accuracy is (81+4)/(90+10)=85%, while the worst-group accuracy is 40% and the group accuracy gap is 50 percentage points. These numbers are teaching arithmetic, not results from an external model. With only ten cases in group B, uncertainty is substantial and should be communicated.
Measure task-relevant errors and denominators

Choose measures that match the task: sensitivity and false-negative rate for screening, false-positive rate for interventions, calibration for probabilities, and task success plus unauthorized-action rate for agents. Show TP, FP, TN and FN counts and denominators for every slice; prevalence changes can make precision differ even at similar sensitivity. Compare with a frozen threshold and report both aggregate and worst-group metrics, not a single favorable comparison.
Quantify uncertainty for small and correlated groups

Small groups have noisy estimates: a 40% result from four successes in ten trials should not be reported as a precise true population rate. Use appropriate binomial intervals or hierarchical methods when justified, avoid normal approximations with very small counts, and resample by independent people, sessions or sites if cases share an origin. Flag suppressed estimates and wide intervals explicitly rather than ranking noisy subgroups as if their ordering were certain.
Check intersectional slices and multiple comparisons

A model might perform well for each broad language or region group while failing their intersection or an unmeasured rare subtype. Evaluate predeclared intersections where authorized and adequately powered, with protections for small cells and disclosure risk. Exploratory slicing across hundreds of groups can produce extreme chance findings; distinguish exploratory hypotheses from confirmatory results and use fresh holdout evidence before asserting persistent disparities.
Stress-test transfer across time and environment

Sagawa and colleagues investigate worst-group robustness for defined groups; the WILDS benchmark tests distribution shifts across real acquisition settings. A strong worst-group score on one benchmark does not guarantee reliability at a new hospital, across changing sensors, or for unobserved groups. Retain time and site splits, document the group taxonomy and assess unlabeled deployment coverage where permissible; updating a model requires a separate untouched evaluation.
Run a controlled reproducible subgroup audit

Proposed evaluation, not a completed experiment: create or select authorized synthetic examples spanning two environments and three prespecified task-relevant slices, split by entity and time, freeze a model and thresholds, then produce per-slice confusion matrices, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, calibration and sample counts. Calculate pooled and minimum observed subgroup metrics with uncertainty intervals across seeds. Register exploratory exceptions and rerun on a sealed test set before claiming any failure generalizes.
Choose mitigations without hiding tradeoffs

Potential responses include additional representative training data, measurement improvements, robust optimization, threshold review and workflow-specific human escalation. Group distributionally robust optimization can target worst-group risk under specific assumptions, but changing weights can also alter average accuracy or other group outcomes. Reevaluate on held-out slices after each proposed mitigation; do not use demographic thresholds or collect protected data without appropriate legal, ethical and organizational review.
Evidence limitations and publication boundary

Oakden-Rayner and colleagues document hidden stratification in medical-image research; Mitchell and colleagues propose model cards with disaggregated performance reporting; Sagawa and colleagues study group-robust optimization; Koh and colleagues introduce WILDS. These works motivate structured evaluation but do not prove any particular deployed product is unsafe. The invented arithmetic and protocol here are educational only and neither establishes intentional deception nor claims a new external incident.

sections: Define the weak-supervisor problem

Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether a capable student model, trained using labels from a less capable supervisor, can outperform that supervisor on independently judged tasks. In the scalable-oversight analogy, humans or weaker models provide imperfect assessments of systems they may not be able to evaluate reliably. This is a measurable performance phenomenon, not a demonstration that the student has learned human values or will remain aligned when deployed.
Separate supervisor, student and independent ground truth

Freeze a weak supervisor W, a pretrained stronger student S and an evaluation set with labels or outcomes independently checked against the actual task. Obtain W's noisy labels only for the training partition, fine-tune S on them and measure W and S on untouched evaluation cases. Without an independent answer key, the apparent student improvement might merely be imitation of the supervisor's errors or exploitation of a flawed judge.
Explain the mechanism without assuming a miracle

Pretraining can give the strong student useful representations and task skill that the weak teacher cannot consistently express in its labels. Fine-tuning with noisy supervision may still steer the student's existing capability toward the target task. Generalization depends on model, supervision error, training method and data distribution; it does not imply a more expressive model always overcomes a weak teacher, nor that improved benchmark accuracy implies faithful reasoning.
Compute a synthetic gap-recovery example

Imagine a fixed test set where a weak teacher reaches 60% accuracy, an independently evaluated strong-model ceiling reaches 90%, and a weak-label-trained student reaches 75%. A simple gap-recovered fraction is (0.75 - 0.60) / (0.90 - 0.60) = 0.50, or half the measured performance gap. These are invented teaching numbers, not empirical measurements. If the ceiling or task changes, the denominator and interpretation change; report raw scores and uncertainty alongside any normalized measure.
Understand why naive imitation is not enough

The Burns and colleagues experiments found weak-label fine-tuning of stronger pretrained models could outperform their weak supervisors, but naive training did not recover all of the stronger models' attainable performance. They investigated techniques including an auxiliary confidence loss. A higher student score could reflect representation transfer, task regularities or training effects; it does not by itself reveal the student's internal objective or make the weak labels trustworthy.
Consider theory without overgeneralizing

Charikar, Pabbaraju and Shiragur develop a theoretical account relating weak-to-strong gains to misfit error under specified modeling conditions. Geng, Hansen and Li examine generalization for linear logistic models under distributional assumptions. These analyses clarify possible mechanisms, but their mathematical settings do not establish a general guarantee for frontier AI agents, adversarial evaluators, high-stakes decisions or every form of oversight.
Design a small, controlled replication

Proposed experiment, not a completed study: choose an open, harmless classification dataset with a deterministic ground-truth evaluation key; train a deliberately weak baseline on restricted labels; freeze three stratified train/calibration/test partitions by source; then fine-tune a stronger pretrained student on only the weak supervisor's training predictions. Compare weak teacher, weak-label-trained student, ground-truth-trained student and frozen strong baseline across at least three seeds, reporting confidence intervals and errors by group.
Audit where misleading gains can arise

Pre-register test items, score the same task and denominator for each model, and examine label noise by class and subgroup. Keep weak-supervisor training predictions out of the held-out evaluation and never use test labels to tune auxiliary losses or prompts. Inspect where both teacher and student are wrong: rare modes, out-of-distribution inputs and hard negatives may reveal an apparently strong average while high-risk mistakes worsen. Include contamination checks and honest uncertainty.
Distinguish task improvement from oversight safety

Even a student that genuinely beats its supervisor at classification may learn unsafe shortcuts, hide error modes or fail when goals shift. Weak-to-strong generalization is a potential component of scalable supervision, not a safety certificate. A separate process must test authorized actions, disagreement resolution, reward gaming, adversarial incentives, distribution shift and cases where no evaluator has reliable ground truth. A benchmark gain is not proof of deception or proof that deception is absent.
Preserve dates and evidence boundaries

Burns and colleagues reported empirical weak-to-strong results in December 2023; later theoretical papers analyze narrower cases rather than documenting newly discovered incidents. The experimental percentages above are synthetic and the audit is only a proposal. This guide summarizes primary research checked November 2, 2026, and does not claim that weak supervision has solved superhuman alignment, nor that a real-world model behaved deceptively.

sections: What a verifier actually verifies

A verifier checks a candidate answer, trajectory or intermediate step against a particular criterion. Some verifiers are deterministic programs such as compilers, unit tests or formal proof checkers; others are learned models that predict correctness from examples. Its output describes whether a specified check was passed, not whether the entire task is safe or a model's internal objective is aligned. Always write down the verifier's exact input and acceptance contract.
Separate hard constraints from learned rankings

For code, a sandboxed test runner can reject solutions that fail public cases but cannot prove correctness on unspecified inputs. A learned outcome verifier scores a whole answer, while a process reward model scores intermediate reasoning steps under a labeling scheme. Combining deterministic validity checks with a trained ranker can be useful, but neither category should quietly become an authority on facts outside its tested scope.
Walk through a synthetic candidate-selection example

Suppose a toy task has four independently generated answers. A learned verifier assigns scores 0.80, 0.70, 0.60 and 0.40, but an independently checked answer key finds that only the second and fourth are correct. Selecting the highest score therefore chooses a wrong answer. With a deterministic independent evaluator, verified success is two of four candidates, and the top-ranked candidate is a false positive. These scores are invented teaching data, not published benchmark results.
Show why best-of-N amplifies verifier weaknesses

In best-of-N selection, when generating N alternatives and picking argmax_i V(answer_i), the system optimizes the verifier's score, not necessarily the true objective. As N increases, candidates may exploit ranking errors, benchmark contamination or fragile heuristics. Recompute true correctness using an independent sealed evaluator as the sampling budget grows; plot selected-answer accuracy against N and the rate of invalid high-scoring answers. More candidates do not guarantee safer outputs.
Understand outcome versus process supervision

Cobbe and colleagues studied learned verifiers that rank generated solutions for GSM8K math questions. Uesato and colleagues contrasted outcome-level and step-level feedback and observed differences between final-answer performance and reasoning errors. Lightman and colleagues found substantial benefits for process supervision on the MATH benchmark with their experimental models and data. These are results in defined math-task settings, not universal proof that a process verifier captures honest reasoning or hidden intent.
Threat-model the verification boundary

Record which inputs an adversarial candidate can control, whether the checker receives untrusted instructions, which files or services it can access, and which side effects are prohibited. Treat retrieved documents, generated tests and model-authored explanations as data rather than authority to redefine success. Run code candidates with network disabled, minimal permissions, resource limits and non-secret fixtures; never allow a candidate to edit the evaluation harness or its own hidden answer key.
Design a bounded reproducible verifier audit

Proposed test, not executed: create twenty synthetic tasks with known answers, four candidate responses each and deliberately planted arithmetic, dependency and format errors. Freeze a deterministic checker and a separately trained ranking verifier. Measure top-1 precision, false-positive rate, false-negative rate and selected-answer correctness under best-of-1, best-of-2 and best-of-4 budgets. Repeat across independent seeds and compare with random selection and answer-only baselines on a sealed set.
Calibrate errors and test adversarial robustness

A verifier score is not automatically a calibrated probability. Evaluate reliability diagrams and Brier or log-loss metrics only when the output has a probabilistic interpretation and the labels are independently reliable. Test near-duplicates, paraphrases, contaminated benchmarks, unusual formats and misleading chain-of-thought explanations. If a small subset receives most errors, show the sample sizes and conditions instead of reporting only pooled ranking accuracy.
Mitigate incentives to game the checker

Use outcome checks that inspect final environment state, independent hidden tests, human review for unresolved policy claims and separation of generator and evaluator permissions. Version the verifier, tests and rubric; track failure clusters and retain counterexamples as regression cases. Avoid training repeatedly on a public fixed suite without a sealed holdout. Reject or quarantine invalid candidates even when their learned score is high; document which failures remain untestable.
Keep the evidence and safety distinction explicit

Verifier research demonstrates that ranking or step-level supervision can improve measured problem-solving under specific experimental conditions. It does not establish that an agent is truthful, that an external action is authorized, or that no reward hacking will occur. A verifier can be incomplete, miscalibrated or itself exploitable. This guide's toy arithmetic and proposed audit are illustrative, not newly observed security incidents or an evaluation of any deployed product.

sections: Mechanism: control flow belongs to the system

An agentic workflow joins a model's decisions to an explicit execution loop: inspect the task and state, choose an allowed action, validate the request, call a tool, observe its result, and either continue or stop. The surrounding application (sometimes called the agent harness) owns the tool schemas, retries, permissions, memory and termination policy. The model is one component, not the entire system.
Fixed workflow versus adaptive agent

A deterministic chain has predetermined stages such as classify → retrieve → draft → check; it may use an LLM at each stage without giving the model control of the next step. An adaptive agent chooses a branch, tool or subtask based on observations. Anthropic describes both patterns, noting the reliability, cost and latency tradeoffs of extra autonomy. Neither label implies that a system performs well.
Worked example: constrained support triage

Imagine a support assistant that first classifies a request, retrieves a relevant order with a read-only tool, and drafts an answer. A refund operation requires a separate human approval and a narrowly scoped write tool; a model's text saying 'refund issued' does not change the ledger. The harness records approval, tool inputs and final state. This is an illustrative design, not an observed production deployment.
Pseudocode: separate choice from execution

At each step: (1) obtain an observation from the sandbox; (2) request one structured action from the model; (3) parse the action against a schema; (4) authorize the target and arguments; (5) execute with a timeout and log the side effect; (6) update state; (7) stop on success, denied action, budget exhaustion or human escalation. Authorization must be implemented outside the model's own instructions.
Concrete applications and boundaries

Useful scenarios include document extraction followed by validated database writes, coding assistance with sandboxed tests, and browser research that cites the retrieved pages. Prefer a simple fixed workflow when the route is predictable; use dynamic tool selection when observations genuinely determine the next step. A long sequence of model calls is not automatically an autonomous agent.
Failure taxonomy: skill, objective and permissions

A missed field may be a capability failure or ambiguous input; a deliberate-looking sequence that optimizes a proxy metric can instead be specification gaming. Tool calls, final database state, observed side effects and the written instruction must be compared before classifying either. An unauthorized call in a constructed test does not by itself establish a persistent real-world goal or intent.
Evaluation beyond happy-path completions

Create held-out tasks with explicit success criteria, forbidden side effects and a fixed tool environment. Record final state, tool trajectory, argument validity, timeouts, token and cost budgets, and recovery from partial failures. Audit false passes from self-reported success and false fails from overly strict exact-match graders. Repeat across task families and changed tool responses; treat a benchmark score as scoped to its harness and tasks.
Security and observability requirements

Use least-privilege service credentials, typed tool schemas, independent authorization and policy checks, sandbox boundaries, rate limits, human approval for irreversible operations, and tamper-resistant audit logging. OpenAI's Agents SDK documents tool guardrails and handoffs, but those are framework-specific controls with different coverage: a handoff is not automatically checked by a function-tool guardrail. Confirm actual behavior in the installed version.
Misconceptions and experiment design

An agent harness is infrastructure for running and observing agents, not a universally standardized algorithm or a synonym for agentic workflow. Adding more tools or loops does not guarantee better reasoning, safety or task completion. Test a fixed workflow baseline against an adaptive variant under the same budget; changes in prompts, tool availability or evaluators can confound the comparison.

sections: Mechanism: represent meaning as linked facts

A knowledge graph identifies entities and stores typed relationships between them, such as (model, trained_on, dataset) or (claim, supported_by, paper). RDF is one common standard: its basic structure is a subject-predicate-object triple. Other property graphs use nodes, labeled edges and attributes. Graph structure supports explicit joins and provenance but does not guarantee factual correctness.
Why a graph differs from vector retrieval

An embedding search ranks items by similarity in a learned vector space; it does not enforce that a specific edge or business rule is true. A graph traversal can require that the retrieved product belongs to an authorized account and that an evidence record supports its attributes. Hybrid retrieval often uses both: embeddings identify candidates, and typed relationships constrain or explain a result.
Worked example: conflicting revenue definitions

Suppose two departments both label a metric 'revenue' while one excludes refunds and the other includes them. A semantic catalog can represent each metric's owning team, formula, version, data table and lineage. When an agent asks for quarterly revenue, it should resolve the correct metric definition and permission scope before generating SQL. A graph alone cannot choose the correct meaning without documented organizational policy.
RDF query sketch and relationship traversal

In RDF-style notation, (reportA, usesMetric, netRevenue) and (netRevenue, definedBy, financePolicyV3) are separate assertions. A SPARQL-style graph pattern requiring both edges can retrieve reports whose metric is backed by financePolicyV3. In a property graph, the analogous operation traverses labeled edges. This is illustrative pseudocode, not a literal query evaluated against a dataset.
From metadata to an ontology layer

An ontology specifies entity classes, relation meanings, constraints or shared vocabulary; a knowledge graph contains concrete assertions that may follow that ontology. NVIDIA Auto Ontology describes generating and reconciling such context from enterprise metadata, exposing it through APIs, CLI and MCP. 'Semantic ontology layer' is a descriptive architecture phrase, not a universally standardized new term or evidence of an independently verified SQL reliability gain.
Applications in AI systems

Graphs help with citation-linked research maps, dependency and supply-chain tracing, organizational data catalogs, knowledge-grounded retrieval, and validation of structured queries. They are especially helpful when relationships, provenance and permissions are first-class questions. Simple keyword search, a relational join or a vector store may be cheaper and adequate for smaller or weakly connected tasks.
Measuring quality before adopting a graph

Construct a gold set of entity IDs, relation labels, source citations and permitted query outcomes. Measure entity-resolution precision/recall, edge correctness, stale or orphan references, query accuracy, latency and cost under changed schemas. Run ablations comparing search-only, relational, graph-only and hybrid retrieval with the same questions; keep evaluation labels independent of graph-generation prompts.
Trust and security boundaries

Treat source documents, inferred edges and automatically generated SQL as untrusted until checked. Attach source IDs and timestamps to claims, enforce access control at the database/query layer, and audit who approved definitions and edits. The NVIDIA Auto Ontology project explicitly notes that its FastAPI internal identity header relies on a trusted gateway; exposing that internal service directly is unsafe, regardless of how useful the ontology is.
Limitations and common misconceptions

Graph edges can encode stale, biased or hallucinated associations; an apparently explainable path is not automatically causal or correct. Store assertion timestamps and source-level review labels to make those failure modes inspectable. Entity resolution is difficult when names collide, and ontologies require governance when organizations redefine metrics. A knowledge graph is not necessarily RDF, an LLM, a vector database, or proof that every generated answer is grounded. Report which links are asserted, inferred or reviewed.

sections: Mechanism: what a benchmark standardizes

A benchmark defines the task population, permitted inputs and actions, scoring procedure, and conditions for comparing systems. The dataset alone is not the protocol: prompts, tool access, budgets, environment resets and grader versions can all change outcomes. A leaderboard is a particular collection of scores, not independent evidence of broad capability.
Defining success and the denominator

For N eligible tasks, observed completion rate is independently verified successes divided by N. Specify whether timeouts, invalid actions, crashes and refusals count as failures before evaluating. When an agent can modify an environment, check final task state and forbidden side effects; do not accept the model's assertion of success as a substitute.
Worked synthetic paired comparison

Suppose two models attempt the same 20 held-out tasks with equal tool budgets. Model A completes 13/20=65% and B completes 15/20=75%, a ten-percentage-point observed difference. This is a toy arithmetic example, not an actual measured model benchmark; twenty cases cannot show reliable superiority without paired outcomes, uncertainty estimates and multiple trials.
What interactive evaluations measure

AgentBench assesses agents over eight multi-turn interactive environments. OSWorld initializes desktop states and uses execution-based evaluators; SWE-bench judges repository patches using tests. These source-published benchmarks differ in tasks, tool scaffolds and graders. A score on one does not automatically transfer to new operating environments or certify safety.
Build a reproducible test harness

Freeze task IDs, initial state snapshots, software versions, instruction templates, tool schemas, evaluator code, random seeds, limits on time and actions, and success criteria. Record action trajectories, tool errors, observed side effects, environment state and resource use. Keep checksums for test manifests and disclose any reruns with a changed grader.
Prevent contamination and metric gaming

Maintain separate development, calibration and sealed test sets. Audit near-duplicate tasks and possible training overlap; repeated optimization against public or leaked benchmark items encourages overfitting. Include distribution-shifted cases and intentional grader probes. Improved pass rates are insufficient evidence of underlying skill if evaluation artifacts can be exploited.
Distinguish failures from grading errors

String-matching a final message can falsely pass a failed tool operation; overly rigid output matching can reject equivalent valid answers. Manually audit a blinded sample of apparent passes and failures, including unauthorized effects. Record evaluator disagreement, tool exceptions and task ambiguity instead of collapsing all outcomes into one number.
Design a fair ablation and report its limits

Compare identical tasks, tools, attempts and compute budgets; vary one system component at a time. Report per-domain completion, uncertainty, safety violations and cost rather than only the pooled mean. Control for sampling and nondeterministic environments. Benchmark results remain conditional on these experimental assumptions and cannot prove general alignment.
Terminology and real-world evidence boundaries

The phrase 'environment-grounded agent benchmark' is descriptive of an interactive evaluation design, not established by these papers as an independent technical standard. Environment-based benchmarking is useful, but an engineered success or exploit in a controlled test is not automatically a deployed incident. Explicitly label illustrative data, author-reported results and independently replicated findings.

sections: Mechanism: the environment supplies consequences

An environment accepts actions, updates task-relevant state and returns observations, and sometimes a reward. It may be a game, software sandbox, tool API, browser or controlled simulator. The agent can see only a partial observation of state; its final text does not itself establish that an intended operation changed the world.
Transition dynamics from first principles

A Markov decision process represents transitions as s_next drawn from P(s_next | s, a), where a is the agent's selected action. The environment, not the agent's narrative, determines what follows. A policy may receive observation o rather than the complete state s, which matters for hidden permissions, stochastic events and partial observability.
Gymnasium reset and step semantics

Gymnasium's reset() initializes an episode, and step(action) returns observation, reward, terminated, truncated and info. Terminated indicates a task-defined terminal state, while truncated may be a time or step budget stop. Treating truncated as task success conflates running out of time with reaching the intended goal; treating it as termination can distort training.
Worked synthetic customer support setting

Imagine states {open, verified, resolved} with actions {lookup, draft, issue_refund}. The environment rejects refund execution unless approval exists, and the agent receives an observation reflecting this refusal. A final message saying 'refund completed' changes no ledger state. This is a synthetic teaching example, not an observed business deployment.
Where authorization belongs

Use typed tools and execution-layer least privilege to enforce permitted actions, track durable side effects, rate limit calls and separate read-only from destructive operations. A model's own policy prompt cannot replace independent permission enforcement. A sandbox also requires isolation testing; naming it a sandbox does not guarantee security.
Why interaction benchmarks expose different failures

AgentBench tests iterative decisions and feedback in multiple interactive settings. OSWorld configures real desktop applications and checks execution results. Such tasks can reveal navigation mistakes or unobserved state changes that a static question dataset misses. Their reported benchmark scores are author-scoped experimental results, not guaranteed performance in production.
Resetting between experimental trials

Record the environment image, dependency versions, tool configuration, evaluator hash, random seed and task setup. Reset state before each attempt and detect leftover files, cached credentials, changed web content or rate limits that contaminate later trials. If a true reset is not available, report nondeterminism and repeat samples rather than assuming independence.
Diagnose full trajectories and possible proxy gaming

Measure final state success, invalid operations, forbidden side effects, step counts, time and cost. Inspect action traces to distinguish capability failure, ambiguous instructions, evaluator false positives and possible specification gaming. Reaching a reward trigger without the intended state warrants analysis; it does not by itself demonstrate deception or an actual safety incident.
Limits and misconceptions

An environment is not synonymous with a reward function, a physics simulator or the unrestricted internet. A simplified world improves repeatability but may omit safety-critical hidden variables and deployed API behaviors. Controlled tests support useful ablations only when those assumptions and permissions are explicit.

sections: The trust boundary at the center of the attack

Prompt injection occurs when an instruction-like string from a lower-trust surface is treated as if it had authority over the assistant's intended job. The underlying issue is not unusual wording: it is promotion of untrusted content into the control plane. Legitimate user requests, developer policy and retrieved evidence have different permissions, even if all three arrive as text.
Direct injection versus indirect delivery

A direct attempt may appear in adversarial user input; an indirect attempt travels inside a page, email, file, repository comment or tool response that the assistant was asked to inspect. Both try to redirect behavior, but the indirect case is especially easy to miss because the malicious text is encountered during an otherwise authorized task. Not every quoted imperative is an attack.
Mechanism: data looks like instructions

Models interpret natural language across concatenated contexts, and delimiters by themselves are not security permissions. A retrieved snippet that claims to be a system message can be semantically salient even though its origin has no authority. The correct system design treats the snippet as task data, applies application-level authorization to subsequent tool calls and prevents model-generated text from granting its own privileges.
Worked synthetic support-assistant example

A user asks for the shipping status of an order. A retrieved product note includes a fabricated instruction to mark the order refunded. The safe path is to summarize the note as evidence, read shipping status through a read-only tool and refuse any refund mutation unless an independently authenticated user request and policy check authorize it. This scenario is invented for teaching, not a reported breach.
Threat modeling and measurable consequences

Describe the legitimate user goal, attacker-controlled surface, desired deviation, trust boundary, available tools and side effects. A model parroting a suspicious phrase differs from an agent making an unauthorized tool call; both differ from an actual ledger change. Record which occurred, not a single undifferentiated 'jailbreak success' label. Data leakage, answer contamination and unauthorized actions need separate outcome checks.
Defense in depth outside the prompt

Prefer narrowly scoped tool credentials, typed parameters, allowlisted destinations, execution-layer permission checks, non-executable document rendering, sandboxing, confirmation for sensitive writes and provenance-aware retrieval. A prompt saying 'ignore malicious instructions' is at best one layer. Input classifiers and sanitization may reduce exposure, but can miss novel payloads or incorrectly reject legitimate documents; measure both errors.
Evaluation protocol using bounded simulations

Construct benign tasks paired with untrusted snippets and explicit forbidden side effects. Evaluate a baseline without attacks, then with attacks under the same model, tools and budget. Log tool trajectories and final state; estimate user-task success, attack success, false positives and cost separately. Test adaptive variations on a held-out suite; leaking the test cases into a prompt or model tuning procedure invalidates simple generalization claims.
Pseudocode for an authorized tool boundary

For each proposed action: validate a structured schema; bind it to the authenticated user and granted scope; reject unknown resource IDs or destinations; request human approval when required; execute in a sandbox; log actual effects; return a bounded observation. Re-parse untrusted tool outputs as data on every loop. This is architectural pseudocode, not a formal proof or a substitute for implementing access control.
Limitations and common misconceptions

Prompt injection is not equivalent to ordinary factual errors, model jailbreaks or training-data poisoning, although these can overlap. A scanner reporting 'no injection detected' does not establish that an agent is safe, and a successful controlled red-team attack is not automatically evidence of deployment-wide compromise. OWASP and AgentDojo describe risk patterns and benchmark settings; mitigations should be independently tested against the application's exact tools.

sections: What makes an injection indirect

In indirect prompt injection, an attacker plants instruction-like material in data the defender will read while serving a legitimate request. The attacker may control a web page, email body, PDF passage or tool-output field but does not need to send a direct message to the agent. The trust failure occurs if source content is obeyed as a higher-priority command.
Entry points and the untrusted-data path

A typical path is user request → retrieval or tool response → model context → proposed answer or tool call. A malicious instruction can sit in search results, a code comment or a knowledge-base entry. The adversary's control is limited to that lower-trust surface; documenting its scope matters because a poisoned tool response is not the same as compromising the tool server itself.
Why retrieval can cross the authority boundary

Retrieval-augmented generation is designed to make external text visible at answer time, not to make that text authoritative about tool use. An attacker can mix legitimate facts with an instruction to change the task or fabricate a policy claim. Cite and summarize the retrieved facts while keeping authorization tied to the user and application; the passage's 'system' label is merely source text.
Synthetic example with a document summarizer

Suppose a student asks an assistant to summarize a publicly available research note. A paragraph within it says that the summary must promote a particular unrelated product. If the assistant repeats that endorsement as an instruction-following behavior, the attacker has contaminated the answer. The invented demonstration involves no actual product or measured model, and does not imply a real incident.
Synthetic example with side effects

A workplace agent reads an email containing a forged instruction to change a meeting time. The correct process is to classify it as email content, summarize what the sender wrote and require the authenticated user's actual scheduling intent and permissions before editing a calendar. Only an audited write to the calendar state would establish an unauthorized action; a model's claim that it changed the meeting would not.
Scope-aware controls and information flow

Separate retrieved text from policy, label provenance in logs and require permission checks at the execution boundary. Restrict what data and tools an agent can access, avoid passing sensitive context into unrelated tool calls, and require approval for irreversible actions. Quoting, delimiters, prompt hardening and injection detectors can assist but are not themselves access control or guarantees.
Evaluation methodology: both goals matter

AgentDojo provides a research example of stateful agent tasks combined with attacker-controlled tool responses and programmatic success checks. For an app-specific test, track legitimate task utility and targeted attack success independently. Use resettable isolated environments and adversarial variants; a defense may lower attack success while also blocking harmless tasks, so measure false refusals and latency.
Worked diagnostic confusion matrix

Imagine 40 synthetic documents: 10 contain planted attack text and 30 are benign. A detector flags 8 of the 10 attacks and also flags 6 benign cases; its attack recall is 8/10 = 80% and its benign false-positive rate is 6/30 = 20%. Those illustrative numbers test the detector only, not the downstream agent's behavior, and are not published benchmark measurements.
Evidence limits and reporting discipline

The 2023 indirect-injection paper reports experimental attacks on selected integrated systems, while OWASP groups a broader class of risks and AgentDojo measures controlled tasks. Neither proves that an arbitrary current deployment was compromised. Report observed side effects, permission failures, version and test conditions; distinguish attempted injection, successful steering, unauthorized action and confirmed real-world incident.

sections: What a learned reward model estimates

A reward model assigns a scalar or preference score to an action, trajectory or generated answer. In preference-based language-model training, a scorer is fit to pairs of candidate responses labeled by people. Its output is an estimate of those comparisons under the sampling protocol, not a direct measurement of truth, human welfare or an agent's objective.
From pairwise judgments to a score

For a prompt x and answers y_good and y_bad, one common model estimates P(y_good preferred) = sigmoid(r(x,y_good) - r(x,y_bad)). Fitting pairwise cross-entropy encourages the preferred answer to have the higher score. Absolute score offsets cancel from this probability; score magnitudes across separately trained models are therefore not automatically comparable.
How the model enters a training loop

A typical RLHF workflow collects prompts and two or more candidate responses, obtains comparisons, fits a reward scorer, then improves a policy against that frozen or periodically updated scorer. PPO can optimize the policy while penalizing divergence from a reference model; best-of-N instead samples several candidates and selects the highest-scoring one. These are distinct selection pressures with different costs and failure modes.
Worked miniature preference example

Suppose a learned scorer gives response A a score of 1.2 and response B a score of 0.4 on the same prompt. The difference is 0.8, so the logistic pairwise model assigns P(A preferred over B) = 1/(1+exp(-0.8)) ≈ 0.69. This arithmetic is illustrative, not a calibrated human-preference probability on an unseen prompt: real confidence depends on dataset, label noise and distribution.
When reward modeling is useful

Preference scorers can provide dense feedback where a direct task reward is missing, such as summarization helpfulness, style or answer quality. They can also rank candidate outputs or guide offline evaluation. Their usefulness is conditional on the comparison dataset covering intended behavior and on evaluation that does not recycle the model's own training labels.
A practical reward-model audit

Record annotator instructions, population and agreement; split data by source/task to prevent train-test leakage; retain untouched held-out pairs; examine performance on ambiguous, adversarial and out-of-distribution examples. Report pairwise accuracy by slice, calibration or score-rank reliability, refusal bias and correlations with independent human judgments. RewardBench supplies research examples of challenging ranking tests, not a universal certificate.
Threats from optimization and Goodhart effects

When a policy selects outputs to maximize a learned score, it shifts its output distribution toward regions where the scorer is high. The scorer can reward verbosity, formatting or other shortcuts that correlate with judged quality in training data. A rising reward score with falling independently assessed quality is evidence of proxy exploitation in that experiment; it does not by itself establish intentional deception by the policy.
Operational guardrails and comparison baselines

Keep an independently evaluated baseline, vary the strength of policy optimization or best-of-N, and plot both reward-model score and held-out human/task quality. Audit high-score outliers and use separate raters, deterministic task checkers or real environment outcomes where possible. KL penalties, diverse preference data and refreshed evaluation can help, but no single knob guarantees that an imperfect learned proxy remains aligned.
Evidence boundaries and common misconceptions

A reward model is not the same as the policy being optimized, and a pairwise preference probability is not a validated probability of correctness. A good benchmark rank does not prove the scorer robust to adaptive optimization, unseen domains or changes in reviewer values. Christiano et al. studied preference-defined RL, Stiennon et al. studied human-feedback summarization, and RewardBench provides controlled reward-model tests; these findings should not be reported as production-wide safety outcomes.

sections: The mechanism: maximizing an imperfect proxy

Reward-model overoptimization occurs when increasing optimization pressure on a learned scorer stops improving and may worsen the intended quality measured independently. The optimizer searches for outputs where the proxy score is especially high, and those outputs can exploit systematic scorer errors. This is a Goodhart-style failure even when no agent is pursuing a deceptive hidden goal.
A causal sequence to check experimentally

First, a reward model is trained on finite human comparisons. Second, a policy is tuned against it or an inference system samples and reranks more candidates. Third, the selected-output distribution moves away from the labels used to train the scorer. Fourth, measured reward can rise while an independent gold-standard or fresh-human evaluation plateaus or falls. Each step must be measured; a score gap alone is not proof.
Best-of-N selection versus RL optimization

Best-of-N draws N responses from a fixed policy and returns the one with the largest model score; RL optimization changes the policy itself to seek higher scores. Both can overoptimize, but they change the candidate distribution differently and impose different sampling, training and KL-control costs. Gao, Schulman and Hilton studied both methods in a controlled synthetic gold-model setup and reported different fitted relationships.
Worked toy selection experiment

Imagine candidate budgets N=1, 4 and 16 produce mean proxy scores 0.45, 0.73 and 0.91 while blinded human-quality estimates are 0.62, 0.70 and 0.58. The N=16 selection improved the proxy by 0.18 over N=4 yet lowered human quality by 0.12. These numbers are invented to illustrate detection, not published model results. Run repeated prompts and uncertainty intervals before concluding an observed reversal is real.
How to avoid confusing scale with performance

Track optimization strength explicitly: N, policy update steps, KL divergence from the reference, dataset size, model versions and evaluation conditions. A raw score from a different reward model or different prompt distribution is not a comparable axis. Use a held-out fixed question set plus new adversarial prompts; report sample counts and confidence intervals, not merely the best single output.
Designing a bounded ablation study

Freeze the reward model and independent judge, hold prompts constant, and vary only N across a prespecified grid such as 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. In a second experiment vary the KL penalty while keeping training data and compute as close as possible. Separate score improvement, task success, annotation disagreement, refusal rate and human quality. Perform blinded manual audits of top-scoring outliers with a rubric fixed before viewing their scores.
Reward hacking, overfitting and misgeneralization differ

Reward hacking concerns exploiting the measured objective; overfitting concerns fitting idiosyncrasies of observed data; goal misgeneralization concerns carrying an unintended learned objective outside training settings. Reward-model overoptimization may overlap with all three, but none follows automatically from another. A model repeating verbosity patterns might be a scoring artifact; use independent outcomes and controlled interventions to test the mechanism.
Mitigation options and their tradeoffs

Potential mitigations include lower optimization pressure, KL regularization, better and more diverse preference annotations, reward-model ensembles, adversarial red-teaming and periodically obtaining new human judgments. Stronger penalties can limit policy improvements; extra judges may share correlated failure modes. Independently verify any claimed mitigation with sealed test data rather than relying on the same score it was meant to restrain.
Limits of the research evidence

The 2022 scaling-law experiment used a fixed synthetic gold-standard reward model as a stand-in for human preferences; it does not establish universal numeric laws for every contemporary LLM or every deployment. Earlier summarization experiments also found that stronger learned-reward optimization can undermine actual judged quality. These are evidence of measured proxy failure under specified setups, not proof of scheming, real-world harm or inevitability.

sections: What an ablation can actually test

An ablation compares a full system with a deliberately modified version, usually removing or disabling one component while holding the evaluation task fixed. The observed difference estimates the contribution of that intervention under tested conditions; it is not automatically the component's intrinsic importance in every possible system.
State the estimand before touching the model

Write a hypothesis such as: removing retrieval reduces held-out answer accuracy under the same retrieval corpus, test split, prompt budget and evaluator. Prespecify the direction, primary metric, minimum meaningful difference and experimental unit. Selecting the most impressive result after examining many alternatives can distort the conclusion.
Retraining versus inference-time removal

Removing a module during inference probes how a trained network currently depends on it. Retraining a smaller architecture without that module probes what a different network can learn. Other weights may compensate in retraining; neither approach alone establishes that a component is necessary in every configuration.
Worked miniature comparison

Imagine a full classifier scores 0.81 macro-F1 and an otherwise matched variant without an auxiliary loss scores 0.76 on a sealed test set: the observed difference is 0.05 F1 points. These numbers are invented teaching values, not published results. Repeat across paired random seeds and report uncertainty before claiming that the auxiliary loss helped.
Interactions require crossed experiments

If two components A and B interact, removing each alone cannot establish their joint contribution. Train four configurations: neither, A alone, B alone and both; compare the incremental effect of A with and without B. A component may appear redundant when another substitutes for it but useful when both are absent.
Fair controls for compute and configuration

Record parameter counts, training tokens, GPU budget, hyperparameter search effort, data selection, seeds, stop criteria and checkpoint-selection rules. A variant given less compute may lose for reasons unrelated to the missing mechanism. Compare fixed-budget performance and matched-quality resource use when the distinction matters.
Statistical and split hygiene

Use identical held-out examples and paired random seeds when feasible, report variation across tasks, and calculate uncertainty intervals. Do not tune the model on the final test set; fit preprocessing only inside training folds. One favorable seed or repeated leaderboard feedback is weak evidence for a robust causal effect.
Ablations for AI-safety research

In a controlled specification-gaming study, vary the presence of a reward-proxy shortcut while keeping the task distribution and evaluation protocol fixed. Measure proxy score and independent ground-truth task success separately, add a placebo change and audit high-scoring outlier trajectories. This is a proposed experiment, not evidence of intentional deception in deployment.
Limits, misreadings and reproducibility

Ablating a module can simultaneously alter input distributions, optimization, training dynamics and model capacity. A performance drop may reflect general brittleness rather than a unique concept; unchanged performance may reflect redundancy or an insensitive metric. Share configurations, source code, seeds, statistical uncertainty and negative results so alternative explanations can be checked.

sections: The prediction-time information boundary

Data leakage means that fitting, selecting or assessing a model used information unavailable under the intended prediction setting. The boundary includes not just labels but timestamps, duplicate rows, correlated groups, metadata and preprocessing statistics. A high reported test score cannot repair a broken information boundary.
Learn transformations only from the training side

Split observations before calculating vocabulary, normalization means, imputation values, feature-selection scores or PCA components. In cross-validation, fit every learned transformation on the training fold and apply that frozen transformation to validation data. A scikit-learn Pipeline helps enforce this separation.
Illustrative normalization arithmetic

Imagine training values 8 and 12 with mean 10, and a future test value of 100. Centering the training examples with mean 10 is legitimate; recomputing the mean from all three values yields 40 and allows the future test observation to affect learned training features. This arithmetic is illustrative and is not a measured accuracy improvement.
Duplicate, patient and document overlap

A random row split can leak when different rows are near-duplicates or concern the same patient, customer, document or event. Use group-aware splits when the goal is prediction for unseen groups, and define the independent evaluation unit before splitting. Near-duplicate prompts and copied documents can make held-out evaluation much less independent than it appears.
Temporal and target leakage

A final diagnosis, post-outcome billing code or later moderation action cannot support a prediction meant to occur before that information exists. Choose the prediction time and audit the availability timestamp for every feature. Evaluate forecasts on later periods when appropriate rather than shuffling across a future-information boundary.
Tuning and model selection also leak

Feature screening, prompt revision, threshold selection and hyperparameter tuning based on final test labels turn that test set into part of the decision process, even if gradient descent never saw it. Use development validation or nested cross-validation for choices, reserve a sealed final holdout and document repeated benchmark feedback.
A practical audit before publishing

For each feature, record the source, collection time, availability at inference and relationship to outcomes. Search for duplicate IDs, shared authors, templates, copied prompts and model-training contamination. Rebuild preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning within each fold, then compare with a simple baseline and report uncertainty.
Leakage in language-model and safety evaluations

Benchmark prompts may appear in training examples, synthetic fine-tuning data or repeated evaluator feedback. Partition by source, time or template where defensible, test newly authored held-out tasks and prevent the grader from revealing expected answers. Contamination undermines evaluation independence but does not itself prove deliberate reward hacking.
How to interpret a corrected score

If measured accuracy falls after removing leakage, the original score was biased for the intended deployment boundary. The corrected estimate still needs uncertainty intervals, distribution-shift assessment and representative test data. Kapoor and Narayanan document scientific ML reproducibility pitfalls; their observations are not a universal prevalence estimate for every study.

sections: The conditional assumption

Covariate shift changes the frequency of inputs: training and deployment have different P(X), while P(Y|X) remains the same. It is a special case of distribution shift, not a synonym for concept drift or label shift. This conditional-invariance assumption is substantive and must be probed, not simply declared.
A concrete deployment example

Imagine a crop classifier trained mostly on sunny photographs and later used on overcast images. Under pure covariate shift, similar measured image features still imply the same crop label conditional on X; cloudy samples have merely become more frequent. If weather changes the labeling mechanism or hides necessary features, the assumption may fail.
Why ordinary validation can mislead

A random held-out subset of the original training population estimates performance on that original population. It need not estimate performance when deployment has a new mixture of input types. Preserve untouched time/site/group-separated evaluation samples representative of the target population, where collecting their labels is authorized.
Importance weighting derivation

Under shared P(Y|X) and adequate support overlap, target risk E_target[loss(f(X),Y)] equals E_train[w(X) loss(f(X),Y)], where w(x)=P_target(x)/P_train(x). This identity follows by substituting the density ratio into the training integral. It does not work where target inputs have zero training probability.
Synthetic numerical experiment

For an invented binary example, training traffic is 80% easy cases with 5% error and 20% difficult cases with 30% error. Expected training error is 0.8*0.05+0.2*0.30=10%. If target traffic becomes 20% easy and 80% difficult, target error is 0.2*0.05+0.8*0.30=25%, even if the conditional error rates within each group remain unchanged.
How to estimate and diagnose weights

Compare source and target feature summaries with an independent sample or a domain discriminator; estimate propensity or density-ratio weights only from permitted covariates. Inspect effective sample size ESS=(sum w)^2/sum(w^2), weight tails, positivity, overlap and sensitivity to clipping. A domain classifier can detect differences without proving that conditional labels are stable.
Choosing an adaptation method

Importance-weighted model selection or empirical risk estimation is useful when shift assumptions and support overlap are defensible and weights have tolerable variance. Alternative responses include targeted label collection, stratified evaluation, domain adaptation, recalibration, retraining or abstention. Each response requires prospective evaluation against a frozen target test split.
What cannot be inferred

An input drift alarm does not establish degraded predictive accuracy, causal drift, adversarial interference or changed goals. Conversely, absence of detected input drift does not establish that labels, subgroup performance or calibration remain safe. Domain matching alone is not proof of reliability across hospitals, devices or populations.
A reproducible research protocol

Declare source/target collection windows and shift hypotheses before inspection. Retain an untouched target holdout, compare an unweighted baseline with weighted and retrained baselines across several seeds, report subgroup loss and uncertainty, and audit data provenance. Treat any performance gain as specific to the evaluated domains, not a guaranteed universal correction.

sections: What out-of-distribution means

An input is out-of-distribution (OOD) relative to a stated training or reference distribution, not intrinsically OOD in every possible context. A new sensor, rare subgroup or novel semantic class can produce different kinds of shift; distinguishing near-OOD from far-OOD requires an explicitly documented reference and evaluation population.
Input shift is not an error label

An OOD flag describes departure from a reference data distribution, whereas misclassification is a comparison with a known label. A detector can correctly flag a novel input that the classifier would have labeled correctly, or miss a familiar-looking input that the classifier gets wrong. Neither score alone proves an unsafe action occurred.
Worked deployment scenario

Consider a vision model evaluated on camera images from one warehouse, then presented with infrared camera images or novel package types. Make separate held-out sets for known packages under lighting shift, unseen package types, and ordinary noisy images. A detector that handles infrared inputs may still miss semantic novelties in familiar colors.
A simple detection baseline

Given class probabilities p(y|x), maximum-softmax-probability detection uses s(x)=1-max_y p(y|x); a larger value suggests uncertainty. For invented predictions [0.95,0.03,0.02] and [0.42,0.38,0.20], the scores are 0.05 and 0.58. This ordering is illustrative, not proof that a model's confidence is calibrated or OOD-safe.
Choosing a threshold without leakage

Select a threshold on a separate development set using explicitly permitted proxy OOD data, then freeze it before evaluating untouched near- and far-OOD test sets. Label which OOD types were visible during tuning. Testing repeatedly on the final holdout and adjusting the threshold would turn an external evaluation into model selection.
Metrics that expose operational costs

Report AUROC and AUPR alongside FPR at 95% true-positive rate (FPR95), false rejections on in-distribution data, stratified recall and coverage-risk curves. With a 1% prevalence of truly anomalous inputs, even a detector with 90% true-positive rate and 5% false-positive rate produces around 9 true alerts and 49.5 false alerts per 1,000 inputs; these numbers are synthetic expectations.
Alternative scores and safeguards

ODIN perturbs inputs and temperature-scales softmax scores; feature-space distances, energy scores and ensembles provide other approaches. Each has dataset, preprocessing and compute assumptions. Separate detection from the policy for abstention, fallback or human review, and verify that routing decisions are authorized and measurable.
Limits of reliability claims

A detector trained on one benchmark may fail on unknown shifts, adversarially chosen data or semantically close novelties. Strong AUROC on a selected collection is not evidence of universal anomaly detection, real-world incident prevention or calibrated error probabilities. Evaluate confidence calibration, classifier correctness and detector utility separately.
Reproducible research checklist

Publish the in-distribution reference definition, dates, dataset provenance, near/far OOD sources, inclusion rules, duplicate checks, model/seed settings, threshold-selection protocol, and a confusion matrix at a fixed operating point. Repeat across different target domains and report where performance breaks; do not claim independent replication unless performed.

sections: What makes an example adversarial

An adversarial example is an input deliberately changed to trigger a model error, with the change constrained by an explicit threat model. A difficult naturally occurring example is not automatically adversarial; intent, selection, permitted transformations and desired outcome matter.
The mechanism in classification

Let f map an input x to a predicted label y. A test constructs x' = x + delta, chooses delta from an allowed set S, and looks for f(x') to differ from the correct label. A small pixel-space distance alone does not prove the semantics or ground-truth class was preserved.
A completely synthetic worked example

Imagine a toy classifier assigning 0.55 probability to a positive class for a vector with coordinates [0.20,0.50]. An authorized perturbation produces [0.18,0.50], changing its decision to 0.49. The 0.02 input change and scores are invented to illustrate a boundary crossing, not an experiment.
Fast-gradient-sign intuition

For differentiable loss L(theta,x,y), the fast gradient sign method constructs delta = epsilon * sign(gradient_x L), then clips to valid input bounds. The sign points toward a locally loss-increasing direction under an L-infinity budget; this is an attack candidate, not a universal proof of failure.
Distance budgets and semantic validity

An L-infinity bound of epsilon restricts every input coordinate independently; an L2 bound restricts total Euclidean change. Neither guarantees that a human regards the modified sample as the same object or that a changed medical measurement remains clinically plausible. Specify encoding, scaling and allowed features.
White-box, transfer and query-based settings

A white-box evaluator may access model gradients; a transfer evaluator generates candidates with a surrogate; a query-based evaluator observes outputs subject to a budget. These imply different capabilities and cannot be compared fairly without reporting access, iteration counts, randomness and query limits.
How to test a claimed defense

Separate clean accuracy from accuracy under a prespecified attack suite, use a frozen and disjoint evaluation set, and include adaptive attacks suited to the defense. One failed gradient attack is not evidence of robustness: randomization, non-differentiability and masked gradients can hide vulnerability.
Safety and scope of conclusions

Adversarial examples show model behavior under a defined input manipulation, not evidence that a deployed adversary exploited the model. Report the domain, norm, perturbation budget, success criterion and sample provenance. Avoid extrapolating from toy images to all text, sensor and agent attacks.
A reproducible comparison protocol

On authorized test data, choose perturbation sets before seeing results, freeze preprocessing and model checkpoints, evaluate multiple attack families and random seeds, and record clean and attacked accuracy with intervals. Audit manipulated labels for semantic stability and publish failure examples without sensitive data.

sections: Robustness depends on a threat model

Adversarial robustness means maintaining a specified property despite maliciously selected inputs inside a defined attack set. A classifier may be robust to bounded image perturbations yet fail under camera changes, distribution shift, data poisoning or prompt injection. Always name the property and attack set.
Robust risk as a minimax objective

Ordinary empirical risk minimizes mean loss L(f(x),y). Robust training often minimizes E[ max over delta in S of L(f(x+delta),y) ]. The inner maximum models an adversary's allowed perturbations; the outer minimum adjusts model parameters. Practical approximations do not certify the true maximum.
Synthetic robust-accuracy calculation

Suppose an invented frozen test set contains 100 labeled samples. A classifier predicts 92 correctly before attack, but only 63 correctly after an allowed bounded attack is applied to each sample. Its clean accuracy is 92% and empirical attacked accuracy 63% for that specific suite, not a universal guarantee.
Threat-model choices that change the result

Specify norm and epsilon, input scale, clipping and preprocessing, test-time access, target selection, query budget and allowed changes to content. For image bytes in [0,255], epsilon = 8 differs from epsilon = 8/255 for normalized inputs; an undocumented scaling mismatch can invalidate comparisons.
Attack strength and gradient masking

Weak or mismatched attacks can overstate defensive performance. Evaluate with well-configured multi-step and diverse attacks, check whether attack success rises with effort, and test differentiability or randomization assumptions. Gradient masking is a warning sign, not proof that a defense has stopped evasion.
Empirical robustness versus certification

Empirical testing demonstrates survival against attacks actually tried; certified robustness proves a bounded property under explicit formal assumptions and computational methods. Neither guarantees reliability beyond the certified region, model version, preprocessing pipeline, class set or operational data regime.
The clean–robust tradeoff

Adversarial training can increase resistance within the selected perturbation model but may require additional computation or change ordinary test performance. Quantify both with matched architecture, training budget and seeds; a better score on one epsilon or dataset cannot establish across-the-board superiority.
Use conditions in safety-critical workflows

Robust evaluation helps when an attacker can manipulate model inputs or when bounded perturbation tolerance is a concrete requirement. Combine it with shift monitoring, provenance checks, access controls and out-of-distribution testing. Do not label a model secure against tool misuse or prompt injection based on an image-attack benchmark.
Auditable experiment and limitations

Pre-register threat model and thresholds, freeze an independent test split, compare a standard baseline with a robust alternative, and test with adaptive white-box and complementary black-box methods. Publish clean/attacked metrics, attack configurations, failure modes, confidence intervals and any untested adversary capabilities.
